title: The “I’m Not Ready for Marriage” Myth
author: Juan Domínguez del Corral
summary: Writing a few weeks after his own wedding, Juan Domínguez del Corral of Simple Men examines a pattern among his male friends: genuine enthusiasm about marrying their girlfriends followed immediately by elaborate postponement until career, degree, or feelings of readiness line up. He grants that real unreadiness exists, such as being deep in vice, carrying unhealed wounds, or being too young and immature, but argues that most 'not ready' claims mask fear of permanent commitment, attachment to the freedom of single life, and the illusion that a moment of full control and security will eventually arrive. His sharpest move is to argue that waiting can make men less ready, because years of building solitary routines cultivate individualism rather than the selflessness marriage requires. He reframes readiness as confidence in direction rather than perfection: a genuine orientation toward holiness, a basic ability to provide, a clear sense of vocation, and a woman one believes God is calling one to marry. The piece closes by urging prudence and prayer alongside honest courage about the real reasons for delay.
points: The author distinguishes legitimate reasons to wait (vice, unhealed wounds, immaturity) from a demand for perfect control and stability before committing.
He argues that a man who says he is not ready at 29 will rarely be ready at 35; he will simply be older and more practiced at postponing.
Extended waiting can reduce readiness, since fifteen years of perfecting solitary routines makes it harder for two people to build a shared life.
Readiness is redefined as a direction rather than a feeling: orientation toward holiness, a stable enough foundation to provide, clarity of vocation, and conviction about the right woman.
For men whose vocation is marriage, he frames committing to a good woman as the path to sanctity, which makes unnecessary postponement a spiritual as well as practical cost.
quotes: This is not an attempt to criticize them —I also thought that way until very recently—, but rather something I have been observing ever since I decided to propose to my girlfriend, and that is that the average male believes marriage requires a long list of things that need to happen before it’s a sensible decision to commit to a woman for life, instead of seeing it as the foundation of stability and real progress.

Not ready” usually means —beneath the surface— fear of permanent commitment, attachment to the perceived freedom of choice of single life, and the comfortable lie that there exists a point in the future when you’ll feel fully prepared, fully in control, and fully secure to make a choice and commitment of this magnitude.
The issue, in short, is that a man who says he’s not ready at 29 (with some exceptions), will rarely be ready at 35, he’ll just be older and more used to postponing.

Consider the logic of it: if two people have spent 15 years learning to be alone, devising perfect routines for themselves, and getting attached to the way they do things, it will be much more difficult for them to create a life together.

However, it’s never about feeling perfectly ready, but more so about being confident in the direction you’re heading toward. You are not supposed to have everything under control or figured out by the time you propose.
Have prudence, pray, and discern your decision properly, but have also the courage to be fully honest with yourself and with the reasons behind your postponement of commitment.
